title: Bicycle: safe teardown
summary: A bicycle gives you wheels, chain and sprockets, steel cables, bearings, inner tubes, tube stock and sometimes a hub dynamo and lights. A bike that rolls is worth more whole. The dangers are stored energy: suspension under air or nitrogen pressure, spring-loaded derailleurs, tensioned spokes, hydraulic brake fluid and the lithium cells in USB lights.

steps.text: Decide what you need before you strip anything. A bike that rolls is transport, and a whole bike on a stand is the base of a pedal generator (build_pedal_generator). Whole wheels make cart and trailer wheels (build_hand_cart). If the bike has a battery pack and a motor, it is an e-bike: use teardown_ebike instead.

Take off the lights, the bike computer and its sensor. Before you charge a rechargeable (USB) light, look and feel for swelling, heat or a sweet smell; if you find any, follow safety_swollen_lithium. Charge it only on stone or a metal tray, watched, and unplug it if it gets warm. Tape the computer's coin cell and keep it away from small children.
steps.warn: USB lights hold lithium cells. Never push a blade or screwdriver into a light's case near the cell.

steps.text: Let the air out of any air suspension before you touch it. On an air fork the valve is under a cap on top of one leg; on an air shock it is on the air can. Stand the fork upright with the valve pointing up and away from your face. Press the valve core with a small hex key and keep it pressed while you slowly push the fork or shock down and let it extend. Do this two or three times, until the hiss stops and it moves freely with no springy push back. Then unbolt a fork or shock whole if you want it.
steps.warn: Wear safety glasses. Never open a shock body or pry out its plug: the sealed part can hold nitrogen under pressure. Leave coil-spring forks and coil-over shocks whole, and never open a shock that stays compressed.

steps.text: Check the brakes. A hose (not a cable) running to a caliper beside a steel disc means hydraulic brakes. Keep each lever, hose and caliper together as one sealed unit: undo the caliper's two mounting bolts and the lever's clamp bolt, and lift them off together. Don't undo the hose fittings, and don't squeeze the lever once the wheel or caliper is off.
steps.warn: Brake fluid is DOT fluid or mineral oil. Never mix the two. If any leaks, wear nitrile gloves and glasses. DOT fluid damages paint, so wipe it off at once. Rinse a splash on skin or in eyes with plenty of clean water. Never pour it on the ground or down a drain.

steps.text: Take the wheels out. On rim brakes, open the brake's quick release first (on the brake arm, the lever or a cable joint). Shift the chain onto the smallest rear sprocket. Open the quick-release lever, undo the axle nuts (usually 15 mm) or unscrew the thru-axle. For the rear wheel, swing the derailleur back and lift the wheel out.

Let the air out of each tyre. Presta valve (thin, with a small nut at the tip): unscrew the tip, then press it. Schrader valve (car type): press the pin in the middle with a small hex key. Lever the tyre off the rim with tyre levers, then pull the tube out, starting opposite the valve.
steps.warn: Use tyre levers, not a knife or screwdriver: a slipped blade cuts your hand and the tube.

steps.text: Take the chain off. Look for a master link (one link with different side plates) and open it with pliers or master-link pliers. With no master link, drive a pin out with a chain tool, keeping the tool square to the pin. With no tools, cut the chain with bolt cutters.
steps.warn: The rear derailleur's cage is spring-loaded and swings forward when the chain comes off. Keep your fingers out of its small pulley wheels.

steps.text: Free the cables. Snip off the crimped cap on the cable end, undo the bolt that clamps the cable at the brake or derailleur, and pull the inner wire out of its housing from the lever end. Keep the housing too.
steps.warn: Steel cable frays into sharp strands that go through skin. Cut it with cable cutters and tape or crimp the cut ends. Brake arms and derailleurs are spring-loaded: they spring open or round when the cable lets go, so keep fingers clear.

steps.text: Undo the derailleurs' mounting bolts with a hex key and lift them off whole. If you take a rear derailleur apart, hold the cage against the body before you remove its pivot screw or clip, then let it unwind slowly.
steps.warn: Derailleur springs are under tension. Released at once, the cage snaps round and small parts fly off. Wear safety glasses.

steps.text: Leave the cranks and bottom bracket in the frame unless you have the right puller. Cranks held by a bolt on a square or splined axle need a crank puller threaded fully into the arm; self-extracting cranks come off with a hex key alone. A frame with its cranks, chain and rear wheel is the drive of a pedal generator anyway.

Unplug a hub dynamo's lead at the hub (Schmidt SON hubs use 4.8 mm flat spade connectors; other makes differ, so look at yours) and keep that wheel whole: the dynamo is sealed inside the hub. For loose bearings, open an ordinary hub over a tray: cup-and-cone hubs drop their steel balls when the cone comes off, so catch and count them. Cartridge bearings are pressed in and stay put.

Only take a wheel apart if you need the rim, hub or spokes on their own. The spokes hold the rim under tension. Loosen each spoke nipple a little at a time, going right round the wheel and round again, until all the spokes are slack. Then unscrew or cut them.
steps.warn: A tight spoke can spring out when cut and the rim can jump, so never cut one. Wear safety glasses and keep your face out of line with the wheel.

steps.text: Strip the frame: seat, seat post, handlebars and stem come off with hex keys. Take a dropper (height-adjustable) or suspension seat post off whole and don't open it: RockShox lists seat posts with the suspension parts that can hold pressurised air and oil. To use the frame as tube, check it with a magnet (steel sticks, aluminium doesn't) and cut the tubes near the joints with a hacksaw. Leave carbon fibre frames, bars and forks whole: cutting or sanding them makes fine dust that irritates skin, eyes and lungs.
steps.warn: Cut tube ends are sharp. File them and wear gloves.

steps.text: Sort and store: oil the chain and bag it, keep bearing balls in a jar, coil cables, and keep tubes and tyres out of the sun. Store lights with lithium cells on a non-flammable surface.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The whole bike, or its rolling frame.** Transport, and with a stand and a motor it becomes a pedal generator (build_pedal_generator).
- **Wheels.** A whole wheel with its hub and tyre makes a cart or trailer wheel (build_hand_cart). Spin it: it should run smooth with little side play. The spokes' tension is what holds the rim round the hub (Park Tool truing).
- **Chain, chainrings and sprockets.** Roller chain with a 1/2 in pitch, such as the Taya 1/2 x 3/32 in chain on the Electra Townie (BikeRoar Townie). It drives pedal generators, grinders and pumps. Check it for stiff links and stretch.
- **Hub dynamo.** A sealed generator in the front hub. Schmidt's SON 28 meets the German 6 V 3 W lighting rule and reaches its 3 W at about 15 km/h on a large wheel. Its output is AC: charging adapters rectify it, and at high speed it gives well over 3 W (SON brochure). Uses: lights, and slow phone or battery charging through a rectifier and regulator. Test it by spinning the wheel with the meter on AC volts.
- **Bottle dynamo.** Clamps on and runs off the tyre wall. Cheap, but with more drag than a hub, and it slips in heavy rain or snow (Sheldon Brown generators). Typical bike generators are rated at about 3 W (Sheldon Brown generators).
- **Cables and housing.** Thin steel wire rope: lashings, tie-downs and remote pulls for gates and latches. Run a rag along it: snags mean broken strands.
- **Bearings.** Cup-and-cone front hubs usually hold 10 balls of 3/16 in per side, rear hubs 9 balls of 1/4 in per side (Park Tool hubs). Other hubs and bottom brackets use sealed cartridge bearings. Spin them: smooth and quiet is good.
- **Tubes and tyres.** Strips of inner tube make strong rubber bands, straps and patches; tyres make wear pads. Let all the air out first and use tyre levers, not a screwdriver or knife, which cut the tube (Park Tool tyres).
- **Frame and fork tube.** Steel or aluminium tube for racks, cart frames and handles.
- **Pump.** A floor or frame pump: test it on a tyre.
- **Speed sensor and spoke magnet.** A reed switch that closes as the magnet passes. It counts wheel or shaft turns, or makes a door contact (build_perimeter_alarm). Test: continuity changes as the magnet passes.
- **Lights and coin cell.** LED lights; dynamo lights run straight from the hub, like the hub-powered Spanninga lights on the Electra Townie (BikeRoar Townie).

## Suspension and brakes: stored pressure and fluid

- Suspension can hold pressurised air, nitrogen, springs and oil. RockShox says not to take one apart until it is fully depressurised, to keep your face away from parts that can shoot out, to wear certified safety glasses and nitrile gloves, and never to puncture, crush or burn an assembled unit (RockShox SID 2020).
- Fox says only its own technicians should open the nitrogen-charged part of a rear shock, says opening a nitrogen-pressurised shock can cause serious injury or death, and warns never to open a shock that is compressed or has not returned to full length (Fox safety 2010).
- Coil forks hold a coil spring: the SR Suntour XCT 30 on the Trek Marlin 5 Gen 3 is listed with a coil spring and preload adjuster (Pedal Power Marlin 5). Leave them whole.
- SRAM says DOT brake fluid damages paint, to wear safety glasses and nitrile gloves with it, and never to pour it into drains, the ground or water (SRAM G2).
- DOT fluid and mineral oil must never be mixed. SRAM, Formula, Hayes and Hope make DOT-fluid brakes (Park Tool BKD-1.2). Reuse a hydraulic brake only with the fluid it came with.
- For a splash of either fluid, rinse skin and eyes with plenty of clean running water. Brembo's mineral-oil sheet says to rinse skin with running water, wash eyes at once with water, and not to make anyone vomit if it is swallowed (Brembo mineral oil SDS).
- Squeezing a disc brake lever with the wheel out closes the pads (Park Tool wheels).
- RockShox groups seat posts with forks and shocks as suspension products that may hold pressurised air, nitrogen, springs and oil (RockShox SID 2020). Leave a dropper or suspension seat post whole.

## Variations

- **Electra Townie Original 7D EQ (2019):** aluminium frame, steel fork, linear-pull rim brakes, a Shimano Nexus dynamo front hub feeding front and rear LED lights, 7-speed (BikeRoar Townie).
- **Schwinn Mesa 2 (2015):** aluminium frame, SR Suntour M3020 suspension fork with 63 mm travel, alloy brakes (listed as V-brakes in one place and linear-pull in another), Shimano Tourney front and rear derailleurs, 26 x 2.1 tyres (BikeRoar Mesa 2).
- **Trek Marlin 5 Gen 3:** aluminium frame, coil-spring fork with hydraulic lockout, Tektro HD-M275 hydraulic disc brakes with 160 mm rotors, 9-speed, 29 x 2.40 in tyres on the larger sizes (Pedal Power Marlin 5).
- **Wheel fixings:** quick-release levers, 15 mm axle nuts or thru-axles (Park Tool wheels).
- **Chains:** some have a master link; to break a worn one with a chain tool, work some links away from the master link (Park Tool chain).
- **Cranks:** cranks with M8 bolts take a CCP-22 type puller, M12 or M15 bolts a CCP-44; self-extracting cranks need none (Park Tool cranks).
- **Derailleurs:** cages are held by a C-clip, a P-screw, a set screw or a pivot bolt; each needs the cage held or let unwind as the spring lets go (Park Tool derailleur).
- **E-bikes:** see teardown_ebike.

## What to leave

- Shock bodies and the insides of forks (Fox safety 2010; RockShox SID 2020).
- The insides of hydraulic brakes: opening one drains the fluid, and it has to be bled before it works again (SRAM G2).
- Carbon fibre frames, bars and forks: leave them whole. Cutting or sanding carbon makes fine dust, and OSHA lists skin and respiratory irritation among its hazards (OSHA OTM carbon).
- Tyres and tubes that crack when stretched, and chains rusted solid.

## Testing what you got out

- **Dynamo:** spin it and read AC volts; the reading rises with speed. Rectify and regulate before charging anything (SON brochure).
- **Chain:** lay it flat and look for stiff links and rust; a worn chain lifts off the back of a sprocket.
- **Bearings and hubs:** spin by hand and feel for grinding or play.
